name: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
title: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
answer: Agent negotiation in over-the-counter markets covers automated software agents that represent buyers, sellers, or dealers in bilateral trading of non-exchange instruments such as bonds, swaps, forwards, and structured products. These agents handle price discovery, quoting, and execution across fragmented venues and direct counterparty channels. The scope includes pre-trade negotiation, term sheet generation, and post-trade confirmation workflows. It sits within agent workflows in finance and overlaps with market microstructure, electronic trading, and regulatory reporting.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Agent negotiation in over-the-counter markets covers automated software agents that represent buyers, sellers, or dealers in bilateral trading of non-exchange instruments such as bonds, swaps, forwards, and structured products. These agents handle price discovery, quoting, and execution across fragmented venues and direct counterparty channels. The scope includes pre-trade negotiation, term sheet generation, and post-trade confirmation workflows. It sits within agent workflows in finance and overlaps with market microstructure, electronic trading, and regulatory reporting.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on low-latency messaging infrastructure, often co-located or cloud-based, with connectivity to dealer platforms, interdealer brokers, and client execution systems. They rely on secure APIs, FIX protocol or proprietary messaging, and data feeds for reference data, credit, and market prices. Compute is typically a mix of event-driven services, in-memory state stores, and model inference endpoints.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by combining rule-based negotiation logic with learned policies for pricing, sizing, and counterparty selection. Agents may use reinforcement learning or supervised models to estimate counterparty behavior, market impact, and optimal concession strategies. Negotiation proceeds through structured message sequences such as request-for-quote, counter, and accept or reject, with constraints on risk limits, credit lines, and compliance checks. Human traders often supervise or set guardrails.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on pre-trade and post-trade controls, audit trails, and model risk management. Automated negotiation can raise concerns about collusion, market manipulation, and unfair pricing if agents learn to coordinate or exploit information asymmetries. Provenance requires recording every message, model version, and decision input for regulatory review and dispute resolution. Firms must ensure agents respect best execution obligations, counterparty suitability, and data privacy rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going is toward more autonomous multi-agent systems that negotiate complex, multi-leg packages and optimize across portfolios rather than single trades. Advances in large language models may allow agents to parse unstructured term sheets and negotiate bespoke clauses. Regulators and industry groups are likely to push for standardized agent identification, explainability, and real-time surveillance. The boundary between human and machine negotiation will continue to shift, with humans focusing on exceptions and relationship management.
